params.question: A newborn presents with bilious vomiting since birth and a double-bubble sign on abdominal X-ray. Which embryological process has failed?

answers.text: Migration of neural crest cells to the duodenal wall

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neural crest cell migration failure affects the distal colon, not the duodenum. Its failure causes Hirschsprung's disease (aganglionic megacolon).

answers.text: Recanalisation of the duodenum after its solid-cord stage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. During weeks 5–6, the duodenal lumen temporarily obliterates. Failure of recanalisation causes duodenal atresia, producing the classic double-bubble sign on X-ray.

answers.text: Division of the cloaca by the urorectal septum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into the urogenital sinus and the anorectal canal. Its failure causes anorectal malformations, not duodenal obstruction.

answers.text: Rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Abnormal midgut rotation causes malrotation and risk of volvulus, not the fixed luminal obstruction seen in duodenal atresia with its double-bubble sign.

overallFeedback.feedback: Duodenal atresia results from failure of the duodenum to recanalise after its solid-cord stage. The obstruction sits below the ampulla of Vater, explaining the bilious vomiting and the double-bubble sign on X-ray.

The duodenum temporarily solidifies during weeks 5–6 and normally recanalises to restore its lumen. Failure of this process causes duodenal atresia, and because the block sits below the ampulla of Vater, the vomitus is bilious.

interactions.label: At the cardio-oesophageal junction, squamous epithelium abruptly meets columnar

params.question: At the cardio-oesophageal junction, squamous epithelium abruptly meets columnar epithelium at the Z-line. In Barrett's oesophagus, what pathological change occurs at this site?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is the reverse of what happens. In Barrett's oesophagus, the squamous lining is replaced by columnar epithelium, not the other way around.

answers.text: Chronic acid reflux drives columnar metaplasia into the lower oesophagus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Persistent gastro-oesophageal reflux causes the normal squamous lining to undergo intestinal-type columnar metaplasia, increasing the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

answers.text: Gastric parietal cells replace the squamous epithelium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Barrett's involves metaplasia to intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, not replacement by acid-secreting parietal cells. Parietal cells are specific to gastric glands.

answers.text: The Z-line shifts proximally due to smooth muscle hypertrophy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The apparent shift of the Z-line in Barrett's is due to epithelial metaplasia, not muscular change. Columnar epithelium extends into territory normally lined by squamous epithelium.

overallFeedback.feedback: In Barrett's oesophagus, chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux causes the squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus to undergo metaplasia to intestinal-type columnar epithelium at the Z-line.
Barrett's oesophagus involves columnar metaplasia of the lower oesophageal squamous epithelium, driven by chronic acid reflux. It is a premalignant condition requiring endoscopic surveillance.

params.question: During development, the midgut herniates into the umbilical cord and returns with a 270° counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery. What is the primary surgical risk when this rotation is incomplete?

answers.text: Hirschsprung's disease with delayed passage of meconium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hirschsprung's disease results from failure of neural crest cells to colonise the distal bowel. It is a separate developmental defect, not a consequence of incomplete gut rotation.
Meckel's diverticulum is a remnant of the vitello-intestinal duct and is unrelated to midgut rotation. It follows the rule of twos.

answers.text: Volvulus around the superior mesenteric artery causing gut ischaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Malrotation leaves the mesentery on a narrow base, allowing the midgut to twist (volvulus) around the SMA. Ladd's bands may also obstruct the duodenum externally.

answers.text: Intussusception of the ileum into the caecum

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Intussusception involves telescoping of one bowel segment into another. It is not a direct consequence of incomplete midgut rotation, which specifically predisposes to volvulus.

overallFeedback.feedback: Malrotation from incomplete midgut rotation places the caecum abnormally high and narrows the mesenteric base, predisposing to volvulus around the SMA and external duodenal obstruction by Ladd's bands.
Incomplete midgut rotation (malrotation) leaves a narrow mesenteric base, predisposing to volvulus around the SMA — a surgical emergency causing catastrophic gut ischaemia.

params.question: During testicular descent, the processus vaginalis — a peritoneal fold — normally obliterates after birth. What results if it remains patent?

answers.text: Cryptorchidism with the testis arrested in the inguinal canal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cryptorchidism results from failure of testicular descent itself, not from a patent processus vaginalis. The two can coexist but have different mechanisms.
Hypospadias results from failure of the urethral folds to fuse on the ventral surface of the penis. It is unrelated to the processus vaginalis.
Correct. A patent processus vaginalis allows peritoneal fluid (hydrocele) or abdominal contents (indirect inguinal hernia) to track along the inguinal canal into the scrotum.

answers.text: Testicular torsion from an abnormally mobile testis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Testicular torsion is associated with a bell-clapper deformity of the tunica vaginalis attachment, not with failure of processus vaginalis obliteration.

overallFeedback.feedback: The processus vaginalis normally obliterates after testicular descent is complete. If it remains patent, peritoneal contents can track into the inguinal canal, causing a congenital inguinal hernia or a hydrocele.
A patent processus vaginalis provides a path for peritoneal fluid (hydrocele) or bowel (congenital indirect inguinal hernia) to enter the inguinal canal or scrotum.
